header.sector: Memory (DRAM, HBM, NAND): supply, pricing, capacity
header.title: Sparse attention does not reduce overall AI memory capacity demand

s01_bottom_line.text: The article argues sparse attention reduces KV cache memory and bandwidth at the SDPA operation but does not reduce overall memory capacity usage, because top-k selection requires the full context in HBM, and system optimizations like HiSparse offload KV cache to host DRAM rather than eliminating it.

The article frames the question as how sparse attention affects memory TAM including HBM and NAND, and concludes the sparse attention memory profile alone cannot portray KV cache efficiency; system optimizations keep memory capacity in play and shift reuse to host DRAM.

If sparse attention does not shrink memory capacity needs and instead shifts reuse to host DRAM, demand for HBM, DRAM and NAND in AI serving infrastructure is unlikely to be eroded by this efficiency technique, supporting the memory TAM.

items.text: On B200, as concurrency rises from 8 to 16 requests, prompt tokens reused from GPU memory fall from 90.3% to 54.8%.
Prompt token reuse from host memory rose from 6.0% to 40.3% as concurrency increased from 8 to 16.
Overall cache hit rate stayed above 95% at all concurrency levels on B200.
GLM-5 routes each token through 1 shared expert plus 8 of 256 experts, giving sparsity of 32.
Sparse attention does not eliminate the memory capacity bottleneck because top-k selection typically requires the full context in HBM.
